hypothesis.cheapest_refuting_observation: python tools/gdl/fnasm.py game/world/items DistanceToClosestPlayer 0x44:0x50 --raw --diff - if the +0x44 `lfs` and the +0x48 `stfs` do NOT use the same register in ours, the load is not shared and the sharing story is wrong. Measured 2026-09-03 on the committed 23-word body: target is `lfs f4` / `stfs f4,32(r1)` and ours is `lfs f3` / `stfs f3,32(r1)` - one register, shared on BOTH sides, so the sharing is real in retail too and the difference is only which register it is.
hypothesis.screened_against_target: yes - the guard and distance registers in both kernels, the four hoisted pre-loop constants at +0x10c/+0x114/+0x11c, the f31 accumulator agreement at +0x1bc/+0x1c4, the fmadds destinations at +0x74/+0x78 and +0x158/+0x15c, and every relocation symbol were read from the aligned raw view against the retail bytes over the whole 122-instruction body.
hypothesis.statement: The remaining work is in the FLYBY kernel, not the loop kernel: 16 of the 23 surviving words sit between +0x44 and +0xdc and NONE of them was probed this run. The mechanism there is a whole-block shift by one register, read from the aligned view: retail assigns f4=guard(sItemZero), f5=distance and computes dx IN PLACE with `fsubs f3,f3,f0` at +0x64, while ours assigns f3=guard, f4=distance and computes dx into a fresh register with `fsubs f4,f1,f0`. The flyby block is the one that also does `sphere[3] = sItemZero;`, so the guard constant's load is SHARED with a store there - which is exactly the coupling that made probe (3) of the v2 record count-asymmetric. The untried idea is to break that sharing WITHOUT creating a second constant: give sphere[3] its own source expression that still reads sItemZero but through a different lvalue (for instance assigning the four sphere members from a local f32 initialised from sItemZero), and see whether the guard's register moves up to retail's f4 and drags the block with it.
